text: Reef life on the Yongala

text: The passenger and freight ship SS Yongala sank off Cape Bowling Green, Queensland, Australia in 1911 and its wreck is now an attraction for divers

text: The SS Yongala was one of several coastal traders that serviced Australia’s major ports. A fast and luxurious vessel, it travelled the populous eastern seaboard, from Melbourne to Cairns. Since becoming a wreck more than 100 years ago, the ship has lain, slowly corroding 15-30 metres underwater and has evolved into a unique artificial reef, now regarded as one of the world’s greatest scuba diving experiences.

text: Mystery surrounded the fate of the Yongala for decades. Before the ship went down on 23 March 1911, it was three-quarters of the way through its 99th voyage in Australian waters. A Marine Board of Queensland inquiry in June that year concluded that the boat was seaworthy, and its disappearance was one of ‘the mysteries of the sea’. In 1947 there was speculation about a sandbank in the area following reports from a naval vessel. The Yongala was finally located by divers in 1958, after a fisherman hoping to salvage something of value dragged a hook through the area.

text: The 110-metre-long wreck lies 20 km inshore from the nearest ribbons of natural hard coral reef. It rests on a predominately flat and featureless underwater area of sand that stretches away in all directions like a marine desert. The Yongala, in contrast, is an oasis. The waters around the wreck ripple with huge numbers of large fish, including many of northern Queensland’s most prized species. Being in a designated marine park ‘green’ zone means that no fishing is allowed in the waters around the Yongala, which has undoubtedly helped maintain the biological richness of the location.

text: ‘You get this amazing abundance of wildlife... It really is mind-blowing,’ says marine biologist Dr David Wachenfeld. This is one of the main reasons the site in the Great Barrier Reef (GBR) Marine Park, due east of Cape Bowling Green, is now enjoyed by more than 7000 divers a year. The site is known for its resident giant groupers that lurk, usually alone, watching territories near cave-like entrances to the disintegrating hull of the shipwreck. Filter-feeding whale sharks sometimes take advantage of the area’s plankton-rich waters, gliding slowly overhead. Occasionally, humpback whales also swim close by as they migrate to or from the areas in the north, where they give birth. And then there are sea snakes, marine turtles, bull sharks, eagle rays and occasionally large manta rays, adding to marine diversity unlike anything seen elsewhere within the GBR Marine Park.

text: The dynamic biological community thriving at the Yongala wreck has resulted from a fortunate combination of events. The currents in this part of the ocean are strong and transport minuscule plant and animal life in the direction of the wreck. While suspended in the water column, these tiny creatures are primed to detect locations suitable for settling, which is exactly what the Yongala is: an attachment site, shallow enough to receive traces of sunlight and bathed in nutrients. These nutrients are washed out to the wreck from the water flowing from the Cape Bowling Green estuary just 12 nautical miles (22 km) to the west and the wreck also fertilises the surrounding water as its metal corrodes and releases iron. It’s a well-known phenomenon that iron added to seawater initiates blooms of planktonic algae*. And wherever there’s lush plant life, animal life quickly follows. Once a few animals settle on a location, reefs can build at a rapid rate. Research has shown that their noises and smells can be detected from afar, much like neon lights of a city, and draw passing travellers looking for a home.

text: There’s equilibrium of sorts – perhaps even a mutually beneficial relationship – that’s developed between the wreck and the community it supports, explains Paddy Waterson, marine archaeologist with the Queensland Department of Environment and Heritage Protection. Growth of the Yongala’s invertebrate life is stimulated by the iron released by corrosion. But the dense covering of life also slows the corrosion process, because it partially seals the ship’s metal from direct contact with seawater. And so, as more and more life has settled on the Yongala, it seems to have helped preserve it, rather than hasten its destruction.

text: From a biological perspective, the most significant feature of the Yongala is that it became a hard surface on an otherwise soft sandy sea floor. ‘Basically, the Yongala has already held together longer than a lot of iron shipwrecks and it’s the artificial reef that’s formed over it that’s protected it,’ Waterson says. Just how well the relationship has worked was revealed in 2011 after Cyclone Yasi cleaned away the soft corals and other invertebrates from the wreck’s upper level, revealing fine details of the ship’s structure beneath.

text: The GBR has more than 2,900 natural reefs and no need for artificial versions. But the extraordinary diversity and abundance of life at the Yongala provides a striking example of the impacts that artificial reefs can have on natural marine environments.
